title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and Peter's Denial
summary: As Passover approaches, Judas agrees to betray Jesus. At the Passover meal Jesus gives his disciples bread and cup as his body given for them and the new covenant in his blood, then teaches them that the greatest must be like one who serves. On the Mount of Olives he prays in anguish, is arrested after Judas's kiss, and is taken to the high priest's house, where Peter three times denies knowing him. At daybreak the council questions him, and he speaks of the Son of Man seated at the right hand of God.
story: Luke's account of the passion, the suffering and death of Jesus, begins here. The leaders who have been looking for a way to kill Jesus without provoking the crowd (19:47-48, 20:19) find it through one of the Twelve. At the Passover, the feast that remembered Israel's rescue from Egypt, Jesus gives the meal a new center: himself, given for them. The chapter moves from table to garden to courtyard to council, and at each stage the disciples fail while Jesus remains faithful. Satan, who left Jesus after the temptation in the wilderness until an opportune time (4:13), now returns. Yet even here Jesus prays for Peter and promises that after he turns back he will strengthen his brothers, which is exactly what Peter does in Acts.
historical:
Passover was one of the three pilgrimage feasts, and Jerusalem's population swelled with pilgrims. Lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon of the fourteenth of the month Nisan and eaten that evening, which by Jewish reckoning was the start of the fifteenth, followed by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread. Luke, like Mark and Matthew, presents the Last Supper as a Passover meal; John's Gospel seems to place Jesus' death on the day the lambs were sacrificed, and scholars have proposed several explanations for the difference. The Roman governor normally came up from Caesarea during the feasts, with troops, because the crowds and the feast's theme of liberation made unrest likely. The date of Jesus' death is most often placed in AD 30 or 33.

The temple officers were members of the temple police, drawn from Levites, under the authority of the chief priests. Luke does not name the high priest here, but he has named Caiaphas earlier (3:2), and Matthew and John identify the house as his. The Sanhedrin, the council of chief priests, elders, and scribes, was the highest Jewish court, though under Roman rule it could not, as a rule, carry out executions (John 18:31). That is why the case had to go to Pilate.
cultural:
At the Passover meal, participants reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, a posture of free people. The meal followed a set pattern that included several cups of wine, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, the lamb, and the retelling of the exodus. Luke mentions two cups (verses 17 and 20), which fits that pattern, though the detailed order known from later Jewish sources may have developed after Jesus' time. A man carrying a water jar would have stood out, since carrying water was usually women's work.

In the Hellenistic and Roman world, kings and patrons liked the title benefactor, a public honor for those who gave gifts and expected loyalty in return. Jesus contrasts that system of status and patronage with his own example as one who serves at table. A kiss was a normal greeting between a disciple and his teacher, which makes Judas's sign all the more bitter. Peter's Galilean origin was apparently recognizable, probably from his accent, as Matthew notes.
literary: The chapter has three main parts: the supper (verses 1 to 38), the Mount of Olives (verses 39 to 53), and the night and morning at the high priest's house (verses 54 to 71). At the table Luke places a farewell discourse, a common ancient form in which a leader about to die gives final instructions, as Jacob and Moses did. It is unusual in Luke's version that the dispute over greatness takes place at the Last Supper. Contrast drives the chapter: Jesus serving while the disciples argue about rank, Jesus praying while they sleep, Jesus confessing before the council while Peter denies him in the courtyard. The Lord's turning to look at Peter (verse 61) is found only in Luke. There are two textual questions. A few manuscripts lack the second half of verse 19 and verse 20, though most scholars accept them as original. Verses 43 and 44, the angel and the sweat like drops of blood, are missing from several of the earliest manuscripts, though the tradition was known to second-century writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, and scholars are divided on whether they belong to Luke's original text.

outline.t: The Last Supper and the new covenant
Greatness as service; a kingdom bestowed
Jesus prays on the Mount of Olives
Jesus mocked and questioned by the council

doctrines.note: Jesus interprets his coming death as given for you and as blood poured out for you, the language of sacrifice. He also applies Isaiah 53:12 to himself: “And He was numbered with the transgressors.” His death is not an accident but the fulfillment of what was written.

The Lord's Supper begins here, with Jesus' command, “do this in remembrance of Me.” Christians agree it is central to the church's worship but differ on how Christ is present in it: Roman Catholic teaching holds that the bread and wine become his body and blood, Lutherans that he is truly present in, with, and under them, Reformed Christians that he is spiritually present and received by faith, and many Baptists and others that it is chiefly a memorial. Each tradition reads this passage carefully in support of its view.

“This cup is the new covenant in My blood.” Jesus draws on Jeremiah 31:31, where God promises a new covenant with forgiveness of sins, and on Exodus 24, where the first covenant was sealed with blood. The new covenant is established through his death.

words.note: Diathēkē, covenant. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew berit, the binding relationship God makes with his people, with promises and obligations. Jesus' new covenant fulfills Jeremiah's promise that God would write his law on hearts and remember sins no more.

Anamnēsis, remembrance. More than recalling a fact, biblical remembering makes a past saving event present and binding for the worshiper, as Passover did for every generation of Israel. Christians differ on how far to press this, but all agree the Supper is an act of remembering Christ's death.

Diakoneō, to serve, originally to wait on tables. Jesus says, “But I am among you as one who serves.” The word gives the church its term deacon, and it defines greatness in the kingdom as service rather than rank.

Peirasmos, temptation or testing. Jesus twice tells the disciples to pray that they will not enter into temptation. The word covers both testing that proves faith and temptation that leads to sin, and the disciples' sleep leaves them unready for the trial that follows.

christ: Here Jesus shows what kind of Messiah he is. He is the Passover host who gives himself as the meal, the servant among his disciples, the Son who prays “not My will, but Yours be done,” and the one who heals the ear of a man who came to arrest him. He knows what is coming and goes to meet it. Before the council, when asked whether he is the Christ, he answers with the vision of Daniel 7 and Psalm 110: the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God. When they ask whether he is the Son of God, his reply, “You say that I am,” is taken by the council as a clear claim. The one on trial is the true judge, and his steadfastness stands against the failure of every disciple, including Peter, whom he has already prayed for.

hard.q: Why does Jesus tell his disciples to buy swords, then say two swords are enough?
hard.a: Verses 35 to 38 are among the most puzzling in Luke. Earlier Jesus sent his disciples out with nothing, and they lacked nothing. Now, he says, things have changed: he is about to be counted among criminals, and his followers will face a hostile world without his protective presence. Most interpreters read the sword saying as vivid, figurative language for coming danger and the need for readiness, not a call to armed resistance. The disciples take him literally and produce two swords, and his reply, that is enough, is often read as a weary end to a misunderstood conversation rather than approval. That reading is supported by what happens a few verses later, when a disciple uses a sword and Jesus says, “No more of this!” and heals the wounded man. Some interpreters think the sword is meant for self-defense on the road, and others that the two swords made it possible for Jesus to be numbered with transgressors. None of these readings turns the passage into a charter for violence in Jesus' name, which his own action at the arrest rules out.

questions: Jesus defines greatness as serving. Where in your life are you more interested in being considered great than in serving?
In Gethsemane Jesus prayed honestly for the cup to pass and then submitted to his Father's will. What would it mean for you to pray both of those things?
Peter failed badly, yet Jesus had prayed for him and gave him a task for after his return. What does that say to someone who has failed Christ?
